programs.title: Put numbers together
programs.provenance: Original AI-assisted teaching; mathematically checked in tests; no educator review

stages.title: Meet the idea
stages.text: Touch each apple once. Say one number for each apple: one, two, three. The last number tells how many. Zero means none. When more apples arrive, keep the first apples and count the new apples too. Addition joins two groups.

stages.title: Try it with your hands
stages.text: Tap + to bring apples. Tap − to take one away. Make 3 apples and 2 apples. Count all five. On the number line start at 3 and make two forward jumps: 4, 5. Moving forward adds one each time.

stages.title: Watch an example
stages.text: Mina has 2 apples. Her friend brings 3. Keep the 2, then count on: 3, 4, 5. So 2 + 3 = 5. Adding zero brings no new apples: 2 + 0 = 2.

stages.title: Try together
stages.text: Use the model. Then tell us what you notice.

stages.title: Try on your own
stages.text: Try before opening a hint. A mistake is a chance to investigate.

stages.title: Use it in a story
stages.text: Picture the situation before choosing an operation.

stages.title: Try a new situation
stages.text: Use the same idea in a different picture.

stages.title: Remember tomorrow
stages.text: Come back after a day. Your finished work stays finished.

questions.prompt: There are 3 apples. Add 2 more. How many altogether?
questions.misconception: You counted only the new apples. Keep the first three too.

questions.prompt: 4 apples and 1 more apple. How many?
questions.misconception: The new apple also belongs in the total.

questions.prompt: 2 apples and no more apples. How many?
questions.misconception: Zero is the number arriving, not the number already there.

questions.prompt: 3 birds sit on a wall. 3 birds land beside them. How many birds now?
questions.hint: Keep the first birds. Count the arriving birds too.
questions.misconception: Both groups stay on the wall.

questions.prompt: Start on 2 on a number line. Jump forward 4 times. Where do you land?
questions.solution: Land on 3, 4, 5, 6. Four jumps from 2 land on 6.
questions.misconception: Count jumps, not the starting point.

questions.prompt: You have 5 shells and find 2 more. How many shells?
questions.misconception: Keep the shells you already had.

programs.title: Equal groups make multiplication
programs.provenance: Original AI-assisted teaching; mathematically checked in tests; no educator review

stages.title: Meet the idea
stages.text: An equal group has the same number of objects as every other group. Three bags with two marbles each make 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. We write 3 × 2 = 6: three groups, two in each group. The total counts objects, not bags.

stages.title: Try it with your hands
stages.text: Change the rows and the marbles in each row. Each row is one equal group. Try 3 rows of 4. Count across a row, then count 4, 8, 12. Turn it around: 4 rows of 3 also make 12, though the groups look different.

stages.title: Watch an example
stages.text: Four plates hold 3 idlis each. Draw four rows with three dots in every row. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, so 4 × 3 = 12. Four plates with 3, 3, 2, 3 idlis are not four equal groups of 3.

stages.title: Try together
stages.text: Use the model. Then tell us what you notice.

stages.title: Try on your own
stages.text: Try before opening a hint. A mistake is a chance to investigate.

stages.title: Use it in a story
stages.text: Picture the situation before choosing an operation.

stages.title: Try a new situation
stages.text: Use the same idea in a different picture.

stages.title: Remember tomorrow
stages.text: Come back after a day. Your finished work stays finished.

questions.prompt: 3 equal groups have 2 marbles each. How many marbles?
questions.hint: Add 2 three times, or make 3 rows of 2.
questions.misconception: Adding 3 and 2 counts group labels, not all the objects.

questions.prompt: 4 rows have 3 dots each. How many dots?
questions.misconception: Rows plus dots per row is not the total dots.

questions.prompt: 2 bags contain 5 marbles each. How many marbles?
questions.misconception: Add the objects in both bags.

questions.prompt: A shop packs 5 boxes with 4 pencils each. How many pencils?
questions.hint: Draw one row for each box.
questions.misconception: There are five groups of four, not five and four objects.

questions.prompt: An array has 3 rows and 4 columns. Turn it to 4 rows and 3 columns. How many dots now?
questions.hint: Turning does not add or remove dots.
questions.misconception: The arrangement changes; the total does not.

questions.prompt: 6 tables each seat 2 people. How many seats?
questions.misconception: Count equal groups, not the two labels.

programs.title: Same whole, different pieces
programs.provenance: Original AI-assisted teaching; mathematically checked in tests; no educator review

stages.title: Meet the idea
stages.text: A fraction describes equal parts of one whole. In 1/2, the 2 counts all equal parts and the 1 counts selected parts. Cut each half in two: there are now 4 equal parts and 2 are selected. 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount of the same whole.

stages.title: Try it with your hands
stages.text: Choose the number of equal parts and tap pieces to shade them. Compare two bars of the same length. Make 1/2 on one bar and 2/4 on the other. Their shaded lengths match. Try 2/3 and 4/6. Unequal pieces cannot be counted as equal fraction parts.

stages.title: Watch an example
stages.text: To compare 2/3 and 3/4, split both same-sized wholes into 12 equal parts. 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so 3/4 is larger. Multiplying BOTH numbers by the same positive number preserves the amount. Adding one to both does not: 1/2 is not 2/3.

stages.title: Try together
stages.text: Use the model. Then tell us what you notice.

stages.title: Try on your own
stages.text: Try before opening a hint. A mistake is a chance to investigate.

stages.title: Use it in a story
stages.text: Picture the situation before choosing an operation.

stages.title: Try a new situation
stages.text: Use the same idea in a different picture.

stages.title: Remember tomorrow
stages.text: Come back after a day. Your finished work stays finished.

questions.misconception: When pieces become smaller, more pieces are needed for the same amount.
Changing only the denominator changes the amount.

questions.prompt: Which is larger: 2/3 or 3/4? Enter the larger fraction.
questions.misconception: Compare equal-sized pieces, not just numerators or denominators.

questions.prompt: Two equal-size ribbons: Arun uses 1/2 of one; Devi uses 3/4 of the other. What fraction of a whole ribbon is the longer used piece?
questions.solution: 3/4 is longer than 2/4. Same-size wholes make the comparison fair.
questions.misconception: More equal quarters cover more length.

questions.prompt: A same-length path is marked in 10 equal steps. Half the path is how many steps?
questions.hint: Split ten steps into two equal groups.
questions.solution: 1/2 = 5/10, so half the path is 5 steps.
questions.misconception: The denominator counts parts; it is not the number of selected steps.

questions.hint: Each fifth is split into two.
questions.misconception: Double both numbers to preserve the fraction.
